case_name: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital c. B.Z.
text:
Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital c. B.Z.

2007 QCCS 4618

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-036972-076

DATE:

September 12, 2007

______________________________________________________________________

THE HONOURABLE

MADAM
JUSTICE JEANNINE M. ROUSSEAU

______________________________________________________________________

SIR MORTIMER B. DAVIS JEWISH
GENERAL HOSPITAL

and

DR. J. PORTNOY

Petitioners

vs

B. Z.

Respondent

and

F. S.

Mis en cause

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

The application

[
1
]

The Court is seized with an application by The
Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital concerning B. Z.. The Hospital is
asking:

•

to be authorized to treat Mr Z. according to the
treatment plan set out in the motion;

•

that Mr Z. be ordered to submit to the treatment
plan and to follow the instructions of his treating physician;

•

that Mr Z. be transported to the Hospital by
force, i.e. by a peace or police officer, should he fail to submit to
out-patient treatment;

the whole for
a period of thirty-six months.

[
2
]

It should be noted that the Public Curator of
Québec is not a party to the present application, nor was it served on him,
contrary to the requirement of article 776 of the
Code of Civil Procedure
:

776.

Every application to obtain authorization from the court or a judge must, if it
is with respect to care or the alienation of a body part, be served on the
person concerned, if 14 years of age or over, and on the holder of parental
authority, the tutor or curator, where applicable, or on the mandatary
designated by a person of full age when he was capable of giving his consent.

An application
concerning a person of full age who is incapable of giving his consent and who
has no tutor, curator or mandatary must also be served on the Public Curator
.

Except in an
emergency, the application may not be presented to the court less than five
days after it is served. No written appearance is required.

The application must be heard on the day it is
presented, unless the court or the judge decides otherwise.

(Emphasis
added by the undersigned.)

[
3
]

In light of the conclusions to which the Court
arrives as to the merits of the application, there is no need to discuss this
deficiency further.

The evidence

[
4
]

The motion was supported by three affidavits and
a medical report. The Court heard the testimony of one of the three medical
doctors who had signed the affidavits, as well as that of the mis en cause, who
is the brother-in-law of Mr Z..

[
5
]

Mr Z. was not present, nor was he represented by
a lawyer.

The affidavits

[
6
]

The first affidavit
was signed by the Director of Professional Services at the
Hospital, as the representative of the Hospital. It is the basic affidavit
which must accompany any motion.

[
7
]

The second affidavit
was signed by Mr Z.'s treating psychiatrist. Besides identifying
the signatory as having status and holding privileges at the Hospital
(paragraph 1), being the treating psychiatrist of Mr Z. (paragraph 2), and
having co-prepared the expert's report, the contents of which are reiterated so
as to form part of the affidavit (paragraph 3), the affidavit is written in
general terms, as follows:

"4.        The Respondent has been diagnosed with schizophrenia
Paranoid type disorder, which causes him to have behaviors which are associated
with lack of insight and poor judgment;

5.         According to the evaluation of the undersigned as well as
the other members of the treating team, the mitigated and unpredictable
collaboration of the Respondent to the treatment is the result of impaired
judgment, in that he denies his psychiatric problems, does not understand their
nature; consequently, he is not in a position to evaluate the danger which may
result from his refusal to be treated the whole being consistent with his
judgment being altered by his problems.

7.         The benefits of the proposed therapeutic plan are
notably, a substantial decrease of the problems presented by the Respondent, a
stabilization of his condition and the prospect for him to be able to function
outside of the hospital environment;

8.         Without the proposed treatment, the Respondent's
condition will likely deteriorate due to medication non compliance and this
will likely further endanger his and other's well being;

9.         It
is in the greatest interest of the Respondent that he be treated in the manner
set forth in the present motion and in the expert's opinion filed as Exhibit P‑1".

The last
paragraph (10) contains the general declaration of veracity which is included
in all affidavits.

[
8
]

The third affidavit
is that of the medical doctor who was present in court and
testified. We learn therefrom that the signatory is a resident at the Hospital,
is a treating physician of Mr Z. and is the co-author of the expert's report
(paragraphs 1, 2 and 3). The next two paragraphs are identical to paragraphs 8
and 9 of the second affidavit, as set out above; the required general
declaration of veracity is contained in the last paragraph (6).

The medical report (P‑1)

[
9
]

It is short:

"May 24, 2007

MEDICAL REPORT

RE:
MR. B. Z.

D.O.B.:
1956-[...]

Mr. Z. is a 50 year old male,
living alone in his house. He was previously married for about 29 years and
divorced 2 months ago. He has one daughter, 11 years old, who currently
lives with his ex-wife. He was diagnosed with Schizophrenia, Paranoid Type at
age 15 and since then has had multiple relapses and re-hospitalizations.

In February 1988, Mr. Z. was
admitted to the Jewish General Hospital with history of poor compliance with
medications, depressed mood, felt life was not worth living, but denied history
of suicidal ideation. Since then, he has been followed by Dr. Nancy Carpenter.

In 1992, Mr. Z. was readmitted at
the Jewish General Hospital after trying to strangle his wife. This was
precipitated by history of poor compliance with medications associated with
violent behaviour towards his wife.

In 2003, Mr. Z. was once again
readmitted at the Jewish General Hospital due to non-compliance with
medications and muttering to himself.

In 2006, Mr. Z. was found in his
home in a coma and admitted to a medical floor at the Jewish General Hospital.
He was diagnosed with sickle sinus symptoms and diabetes mellitus. A pacemaker
was inserted and he was given insulin. Endocrinology was consulted and
pacemaker clinic follow-up was arranged. Mr. Z. did not attend his follow-up
appointments regularly.

On May 2, 2007, Mr. Z. was
readmitted at the Jewish General Hospital after stopping his medications with a
history of threatening brother-in-law with a knife, making threatening calls to
brother-in-law and his wife. He also disturbed the neighbours and damaged their
properties.

Mr. Z. remains an in-patient at the
Jewish General Hospital with poor insight and judgement. He states that he was
stressed by his brother-in-law knocking on his window and came out of the house
with a pocket knife to make a point that he had had enough, but didn't intend
to use the knife. He also reported that neighbours put rusty pipes in his house
and they keep sending him messages.

Because of the history of
non-compliance with treatment and subsequent inevitable decompensations, during
which Mr. Z. becomes psychotic, paranoid and violent, it is our opinion that
Mr. Z. represents a serious risk of self-harm and harm to others when not
treated. This is further complicated by total lack of insight into his
condition. For these reasons (history of non-compliance, severe psychotic and
dangerous relapses and positive response to treatment), we are requesting that
Mr. Z. be placed under:

1.         Out-Patient Compulsory Treatment:

Risperidal 2 mg po QAM & 3 mg po QHS or IM equivalent

Effexor XR 150 mg po qd

Benztropin
2 mg po QD

2.         Comply with follow-up therapy in our Out-Patient
Department.

3.         Placement in a supervised living setting if deemed
necessary.

4.         Be brought back by police and/or Urgence Santé in case of
non-compliance for psychiatric evaluation.

Sincerely,

Signed: K. Geagea

Signed: S.
Aljadidi

_______________                                                        ________________

K.
Geagea, M.D.                                                           S.
Aljadidi, R‑1

Director,

In-Patient
Services"

The medical testimony before the Court

[
10
]

No psychiatrist testified before the Court, nor
were any present before the Court. This, in itself, is surprising.

[
11
]

The Hospital chose to present as its sole
medical witness a first-year resident, a medical doctor with three years of
practice but who had not yet even finished the first of the five years of
residency in psychiatry.

[
12
]

As a general principle, a first-year resident is
not an expert in psychiatry and should not be offered as such, nor asked to
testify as such, even though no formal attempt was made to qualify her as an
expert witness. It is unfair to the resident and also tends to indicate that
the legal proceedings involved are not being taken seriously by the applicants.

[
13
]

Thus, during the testimony, whenever the medical
witness is asked a question which begins with: "In your experience,
Doctor, …", the opinion proffered is based on nine or ten months of
experience.

[
14
]

The Court cannot give much weight to such
testimony.

The testimony of F. S.

[
15
]

F. S. is Mr. Z.'s brother-in-law: he is the
widower of Mr. Z.'s older sister. Mr S. is 64 years old and has known Mr Z. for
about forty years; when they met, Mr Z. was 9 years old; he is now 50 years
old.

[
16
]

Mr S.'s testimony was very useful. Due to his
long-time involvement with the Z. family, he was able to provide background
information and an overall view of the situation.

[
17
]

Moreover, Mr S. is one of the three trustees of
a trust fund set up by Mr Z.'s mother's testament, the beneficiary of which is
Mr Z.. As such, he is involved in the management of Mr Z.'s assets.

[
18
]

Pursuant to recent events, Mr S. had become
concerned enough to consult a lawyer, who also represented him in the present
proceedings, concerning the possibility of a curatorship, so that Mr Z. could
move to a residence with some kind of supervision and help.

[
19
]

In summary, Mr S. was a credible and useful
witness.

The Court's analysis

[
20
]

We shall, first of all, review the relevant
principles of law, before examining whether or not, or to what extent, the
facts as proven are sufficient to give rise to the judgment being requested by
the Hospital.

The principles of law

[
21
]

The fundamental principle is that of the
integrity of each human being. That is the starting point. Not for nothing are
the relevant articles situated at the very beginning of the
Civil Code of
Québec
.

[
22
]

The second title of Book One of the Code deals
with "Certain personality rights". The first chapter deals with
"Integrity of the person".

[
23
]

First, the principle is enunciated:

10.

Every person is inviolable and is entitled to the integrity of his person.

Except
in cases provided for by law, no one may interfere with his person without his
free and enlightened consent.

[
24
]

Thereafter, two particular situations are dealt
with, being "cases provided for by law":

•

in Section I, "Care" — « Des Soins »;

•

in Section II, "Confinement in an
institution and psychiatric assessment" — « De la garde en
établissement et de l'évaluation psychiatrique ».

[
25
]

We are concerned with the first section, which
deals with the care to be provided to someone who is unable to give a valid
consent:

11.

No person may be made to undergo care of any nature, whether for examination,
specimen taking, removal of tissue, treatment or any other act, except with his
consent.

If
the person concerned is incapable of giving or refusing his consent to care, a
person authorized by law or by mandate given in anticipation of his incapacity
may do so in his place.

[
26
]

At this point, we arrive at the central issue,
i.e. a person's capacity to give a valid consent.

[
27
]

The 1994 decision of the Court of Appeal
[1]
discusses this issue. There are set out
therein five aspects to be considered:

1.   "La personne comprend-elle la nature de la
maladie pour laquelle un traitement lui est proposé?";

2.   "La personne comprend-elle la nature et le
but du traitement?";

3.   "La personne saisit-elle les risques et les
avantages du traitement si elle le subit?";

4.   "La personne comprend-elle les risques de ne
pas subir le traitement?";

5.   "La capacité de comprendre de la personne
est-elle affectée par sa maladie?".

[
28
]

Once the person's inability to give a valid
consent is established, a substitute consent must be obtained. There are two
possible sources:

•

either someone close to the patient, or

•

the Superior Court.

[
29
]

Article 15 C.C.Q. sets out the list of
substitute
consent givers
who are
close to the patient
: first of all the
mandatory, tutor or curator; if there are none, the patient's spouse; if none,
a close relative or a person who shows a special interest in the patient.
Article 15 C.C.Q. reads as follows:

15.
Where it is ascertained that a person of full age is incapable of
giving consent to care required by his or her state of health, consent is given
by his or her mandatary, tutor or curator. If the person of full age is not so
represented, consent is given by his or her married, civil union or
de facto

spouse or, if the person has no spouse or his or her spouse is prevented from
giving consent, it is given by a close relative or a person who shows a special
interest in the person of full age.

[
30
]

Article 16 C.C.Q. sets out the circumstances
when
the Superior Court
's involvement is required:

16.

The
authorization of the court is
necessary where the person who may give consent
to care required by the state of health of a minor or a person of full age who
is incapable of giving his consent is prevented from doing so or, without
justification, refuses to do so; it is also
required where a person of full
age who is incapable of giving his consent categorically refuses to receive
care
, except in the case of hygienic care or emergency.

The authorization of the court is necessary,
furthermore, to cause a minor 14 years of age or over to undergo care he
refuses, except in the case of emergency if his life is in danger or his
integrity threatened, in which case the consent of the person having parental
authority or the tutor is sufficient.

(Emphasis
added.)

[
31
]

In the present case, we are interested in the
first paragraph of article 16 C.C.Q. It contemplates two sets of circumstances:

•

absence or refusal of consent by the appropriate
consent giver who is close to the patient, as enumerated in article 15 C.C.Q.;

•

refusal by the patient to receive the necessary
care.

[
32
]

Article 16 C.C.Q. was analyzed by the Court of
appeal in 1994, in the same decision as the one referred to above in paragraph
27
[2]
. The Court of Appeal pointed out that when
the patient who is unable to give a valid consent refuses to submit to
appropriate care, the authorization of the Superior Court is required.
It is
the patient's refusal which triggers the need for a judicial authorization
:

"Ces articles révèlent
également les deux points importants suivants:

a) […]

b)
même après que l'inaptitude de la personne majeure à consentir à des soins
médicaux requis par son état de santé a été constatée et que le consentement
substitué a été obtenu, l'autorisation du tribunal est de plus requise si la
personne inapte refuse catégoriquement de recevoir les soins; c'est ce qu'énonçait
la dernière partie de l'article 19.4 C.c.B.-C., maintenant la dernière partie
du premier alinéa de l'
article 16

C.c.Q.
; dans ce cas, il appartiendra à la
personne justifiant un intérêt suffisant de convaincre le tribunal du
bien-fondé de la constatation d'inaptitude et de la nécessité des soins
suggérés."
[3]

[
33
]

The Court of Appeal later comes to the
conclusion in the same decision that once the patient refuses care, judicial
authorization must be sought, regardless of whether or not the opinion of the
substitute consent giver who is close to the patient was sought:

"L'appelant a agi
correctement.

Dès le moment où une personne
majeure jugée inapte par un médecin refuse de recevoir des soins requis par son
état de santé, il devient superflu, si leur consentement n'a pas déjà été
obtenu, de s'adresser aux personnes substituées, car ou bien leur consentement
est donné ou bien il est refusé. Dans le premier cas, le consentement entre
indéniablement en conflit avec le refus du patient et, dans le deuxième cas, il
devient le refus injustifié dont parle l'article 19.4 C.c.B.‑C., devenu
l'
article 16

C.c.Q.
(il ne faut pas perdre de vue la qualité des soins en
cause: « requis par l'état de santé »). Dans l'un et l'autre de ces
cas, l'autorisation du tribunal est nécessaire; de toute façon, le tribunal
prendra l'avis de ces personnes substituées, comme lui commande maintenant
l'
article 23
C.c.Q. :

Le tribunal appelé à
statuer sur une demande d'autorisation relative à des soins […] prend l'avis
d'experts, du titulaire de l'autorité parentale, du mandataire, du tuteur ou du
curateur et du conseil de tutelle; il peut aussi prendre l'avis de toute
personne qui manifeste un intérêt particulier pour la personne concernée par la
demande.

Il est aussi tenu,
sauf impossibilité, de recueillir l'avis de cette personne et, à moins qu'il ne
s'agisse de soins requis par son état de santé, de respecter son refus.

Devant le refus de la personne
majeure inapte, une partie du rôle du médecin est déléguée au tribunal qui, une
fois l'inaptitude constatée, statuera en même temps sur l'autorisation.

En conclusion, qu'un consentement substitué ait ou non été obtenu,
lorsque le majeur inapte refuse catégoriquement de recevoir les soins requis
par son état de santé, une autorisation du tribunal pour passer outre à ce
refus doit être obtenue
."
[4]

(References omitted.)

(Emphasis added.)

[
34
]

To summarize: the intervention of the Superior
Court is required if the patient refuses appropriate care. Let us now look at
the evidence concerning Mr Z. in that regard.

Mr Z.'s approach as to the care suggested

[
35
]

What is Mr Z.'s situation at the present time?
He was admitted to the Hospital on May 2 and was still an in-patient at the
time of the hearing, on June 6, 2007.

[
36
]

When he was first hospitalized, Mr Z. refused to
be treated. He subsequently agreed and became receiving appropriate medication.
His condition improved.

[
37
]

Mr Z. is now compliant. The testimony of the
medical doctor was clear on that point.

[
38
]

Moreover, the day before the hearing, he met
with his brother-in-law, the Hospital's lawyer, his treating psychiatrist and
the first-year resident. He informed them that he did not want to be
represented by a lawyer, that he agreed with the motion and did not want to
come to court to attend the hearing.

[
39
]

The Court can only conclude that Mr Z. is
not

"categorically
[refusing] to receive care"
.

[
40
]

It should be noted that a close reading of the
motion and of the medical report do not indicate present day or contemporary
refusal of treatment as the basis for the judicial authorization. The relevant
allegations are couched in language which deals in generalities; see paragraph
7:

"7.   Respondent
when ill always denies the existence of his psychiatric troubles; consequently,
he does not cooperate in accepting adequate treatment and has not always
complied with outpatient treatment."

and state
concerns about future non-compliance: see paragraphs 11 and 14 of the motion
and paragraphs 8 and 4 of the second and third affidavits.

[
41
]

The medical report is to the same effect:
"Because of
the history of non-compliance with treatment …"
(P‑1 reproduced above at paragraph 9).

[
42
]

In summary, Mr Z. is sick but he is not now,
i.e. at the time of the signature of the motion and of the hearing, refusing
treatment. The Court is of the opinion the conditions are not met to give it
jurisdiction.

[
43
]

But what of his anticipated non-compliance?

Future non-compliance

[
44
]

Part of the Hospital's arguments was as follows:
we want to have this order in case we need it in the future; we will put it in
the file and hope we don't have to use it; but if Mr Z. is not compliant, we
will already have it.

[
45
]

The Court refers to the 2004 comments of
Chamberland J.C.A., which condemn such an approach. The medical facts in that
case are different from those which concern us here, but the principle is the
same:

"
L'ordonnance relative aux
médicaments

À ce sujet, le juge de première
instance note que l'appelante accepte maintenant – en fait, depuis son
hospitalisation en mars 2003 – de prendre les médicaments qui lui sont
prescrits; il prononce toutefois l'ordonnance recherchée « pour éviter des
démarches répétitives au cas de refus de sa part ».

Cette ordonnance se heurte, à mon
avis, à deux problèmes.

Premièrement, le médecin traitant
de l'appelante, le Dr Marceau, estime que sa patiente est tout à fait apte à
consentir à la prise des médicaments qu'on lui propose; deuxièmement,
l'appelante, loin d'opposer un refus catégorique, accepte de les prendre depuis
qu'elle est hospitalisée.

Les conditions posées par l'
article
16

C.c.Q.
pour justifier l'intervention d'un juge ne sont donc pas satisfaites.

Dans ce contexte, et même si la décision du juge peut se justifier
en termes de rapidité, d'efficacité et d'économie, il n'est pas permis de
l'entériner sur le plan du droit. Le respect de l'autonomie, de l'inviolabilité
et de l'intégrité de la personne est une valeur fondamentale du droit québécois
en matière de soins. Il n'y a rien dans la lettre et l'esprit de la loi qui
permette d'évaluer à l'avance une demande future advenant un refus et d'en décider.
La situation peut évoluer entre aujourd'hui et demain; il est imprudent, et
contraire à la loi, de décider aujourd'hui en fonction d'une situation qui
risque de se présenter demain."
[5]

(References omitted.)

Summary

[
46
]

In summary, the facts presented are not
sufficient in law to contemplate the authorization sought. This is sufficient
to dismiss the motion.

[
47
]

Some aspects of the application however merit
further comment.

Further comments

The medical evidence

[
48
]

It is thin and unconvincing.

[
49
]

Let us first look at the medical report (P‑1),
which is reproduced above in its entirety. The diagnosis is set out in the
first paragraph:
"He was diagnosed with Schizophrenia, Paranoid
Type at age 15 and since then has had multiple relapses and
re-hospitalizations"
.

[
50
]

The diagnosis itself is not contested. However,
the evidence does not support the statement of "multiple relapses and
re-hospitalizations".

[
51
]

Over the last thirty-five years, since his
diagnosis at age 15, Mr Z. had to be hospitalized five times: in 1988, 1992,
2003, 2006 and 2007; there were crises due to poor compliance with medication,
which allowed symptoms to manifest themselves: depression, violence against his
wife, mistrust of neighbours and family.

[
52
]

What the evidence shows clearly is that while he
and his wife were living together, she took care of him; she looked out for
him; no one knew him better than she did; when he was not well and help was
needed, she would get in touch with her brother-in-law, Mr S..

[
53
]

The testimony of Mr S. is clear and convincing
on that subject.

[
54
]

Thus, from 1971, when Mr Z. was first diagnosed
as suffering from schizophrenia, until 1988, when he was first admitted to the
Hospital in his early thirties, he was able to function with the help and
support of his wife and family during those seventeen years.

[
55
]

Over the next fifteen years, there were two
crises: in 1992 and another, eleven years later in 2003. In between time, while
he was living with his wife and their young daughter, Mr Z. must have been able
to function.

[
56
]

Thus, the statement of "multiple"
relapses and re-hospitalizations for the three crises during the 1971-2006
timeframe appears to the Court to be a bit excessive.

[
57
]

The 2006-2007 timeframe is different. It is true
that Mr Z. had to be hospitalized twice. Both times, he had stopped taking his
medication; in 2006, the specific date being unknown, he was found in a coma
and in May 2007, he had become aggressive.

[
58
]

But one must not forget that Mr Z. was then
living alone. He and his wife had separated; divorce proceedings were underway.

[
59
]

In summary, while he and his wife were living
together, Mr Z.'s condition was generally under control. Since their separation
a year and a half ago, he had deteriorated to a serious degree.

The authorization being sought

[
60
]

The problem
is
someone who, left to his own devices, will most probably not take his
medication and whose mental state will deteriorate.

[
61
]

The proposed solution
is to allow police officers to go and get Mr Z. if he does not show
up at the Hospital for his appointments and to bring him to the Hospital.

[
62
]

What reason
is
given for this approach? Why does the Hospital want to be able to bring Mr Z.
back by force if he does not respect his appointments?

[
63
]

One might expect that it would be so as to
administer the appropriate medication to Mr Z., if tests showed he had stopped
taking his medication. But that is not the purpose, as the motion contains no
conclusions dealing with the forced administration of medication should Mr Z.
refuse to comply once brought to the Hospital by the police.

[
64
]

So why does the Hospital want to be able to have
its patient forcibly brought back? Part of the answer appears only in the
medical report (P‑1) as reproduced above at paragraph 9:

"4.        Be brought back by police and/or Urgence Santé in
case of non-compliance
for psychiatric evaluation
."

(Emphasis
added.)

the rest
appears in the conclusion dealing with police assistance, which reads as
follows:

"ORDER that in the event the Respondent fails to submit to
out-patient treatment, he be transported by a peace officer or a police officer
to the Sir Mortimer B. Davis – Jewish General Hospital
so that treatment may
be continued within the briefest delay, in order to prevent a psychotic
relapse, dangerous behavior and a re hospitalization;
"

(Emphasis
added.)

[
65
]

Thus, the Hospital wants to prevent a psychotic
relapse but is not asking to be authorized to treat Mr Z. against his will. And
of course it cannot, because Mr Z. is not refusing treatment.

[
66
]

But had the Hospital wanted to be authorized to
treat Mr Z. against his will, the conclusions of its motion would have
contemplated the administration of medication by intramuscular injection, such
as was requested in
Hôpital Général Juif Sir Mortimer B. Davis
vs
B.K.
[6]
, or, generally, the assistance of a police
or peace officer, or an ambulance attendant, to carry out the authorized
treatment by force.

[
67
]

One can also refer to the following conclusions
found in other cases:

•

"AUTORISE les
demandeurs ou toute personne ou tout établissement désigné par eux à traiter le
défendeur, A…T…, malgré son refus catégorique et contre son gré, pour une
période de deux (2) ans à compter du présent jugement, en lui administrant les
traitements suivants, selon les dosages et les fréquences à être prescrits et
ajustés par les médecins traitants et soit, plus particulièrement:

un traitement antipsychotique administré
par la bouche ou par voie intramusculaire advenant un refus du défendeur;

au besoin, une médication psychoactive de
type stabilisatrice d'humeur ou anxiolytique (un benzodiazépine);

AUTORISE les demandeurs ou toute personne
ou tout établissement désigné par eux à administrer au défendeur, A… T…, la
médication requise pour contrer les éventuels effets secondaires qu'il pourrait
subir, selon les dosages et les fréquences à être prescrits et ajustés par les médecins
traitants du défendeur, compte tenu de la réaction de ce dernier à ces
traitements;

[…]

AUTORISE tout agent de la paix, ambulancier ou toute autre ressource
d'assister les demandeurs ou toute personne choisie par eux dans l'exécution
desdites autorisations, sur simple demande verbale de ceux-ci et ce, quel que
soit le lieu où se trouve le défendeur, y compris le transport du défendeur au
Centre hospitalier …;"
[7]

•

"ORDONNE à Mme C…
C… de se soumettre aux traitements, thérapies, examens et prélèvements suivants
et ce, même en externe :

a)   Examens préliminaires et
examens de suivi nécessaires à l'utilisation de Zyprexa et de Clozapine;

b)   Prélèvements biologiques
nécessaires au suivi thérapeutique;

c)   Prise de Zyprexa et
Clozapine;

[…]

AUTORISE la demanderesse, ses médecins, psychiatres et préposés à
utiliser la force raisonnable pour faire respecter la présente
ordonnance;"
[8]

•

"AUTORISE la
demanderesse ou tout autre médecin appelé à la remplacer à traiter le
défendeur, malgré son refus catégorique et contre son gré, selon le plan de
soins suivant et pour une durée de deux ans à compter du présent jugement, sauf
si à l'intérieur de ce délai un médecin constate l'aptitude du défendeur à
consentir à ce traitement:

a)   un traitement pharmacologique ayant
pour objet une ou des médications antipsychotiques (par voie orale ou par
injection);

b)   un traitement pharmacologique ayant
pour objet une ou des médications (par voie orale ou par injection) visant à
atténuer ou combattre les effets secondaires de la médication antipsychotique;

c)   les prises de sang, bilans, tests et
autres examens physiques permettant le contrôle des paramètres biologiques
nécessaires lors du traitement avec les médicaments ainsi que lors du contrôle
de sa condition physique;

et ce, en recourant à tous moyens pour les administrer, y compris la
force si nécessaire"
[9]
.

[
68
]

In the conclusions sought in the present case,
there is nothing to that effect; the only reference to outside force concerns
the transportation of Mr Z. to the Hospital.

[
69
]

Could this simply be an oversight or the result
of inadequate drafting? The answer is no: twice, the Court asked the medical
doctor; the issue was also brought up by the Court during pleadings.

[
70
]

In summary, the Hospital, being of the opinion
that Mr Z. is incapable of giving his consent to being treated, wants to treat
Mr Z. in the manner set out in the conclusions. Fine.

[
71
]

The Hospital expects Mr Z. not to comply with
his treatment on an out-patient basis; in other words, the Hospital does not
expect Mr Z. to show up regularly for his appointments. If Mr Z. does not show
up for his appointments on a regular basis, the Hospital shall not be able to
monitor his compliance and his state of mind. Thus the Hospital wants to be
able to go and get Mr Z..

[
72
]

In other words, the Hospital wants to be able to
keep track of Mr Z. and of his compliance or non-compliance without asking to
be able to treat him by force if necessary. This is not possible.

The alternative: a supervised living setting

[
73
]

This conclusion suffers from the same problem as
the one discussed above, i.e. the use of force to bring Mr Z. back to the
Hospital: as the Hospital and its doctors are not asking to be authorized to
treat Mr Z. against his will, they cannot control his movements nor his choice
of residence!

[
74
]

In other words, living in a supervised facility
may well be part of a treatment plan, but it can be ordered by the Superior
Court only if the Superior Court has jurisdiction. And, in the present case, as
explained above, the Superior Court does not have jurisdiction.

[
75
]

This does not mean that it would not be in Mr Z.'s
interest to live in some kind of a residence, where support would be available.
Such a setting would replicate, to a certain extent, the situation which
prevailed during all the years when Mr Z. lived with his wife and she looked
out for him.

[
76
]

The Court notes that Mr S. had already initiated
contacts with a lawyer to begin proceedings for some kind of protective
supervision; when the Hospital got involved with the present motion, Mr S. put
his own proceedings on hold.

[
77
]

During the hearing, the Court stated that the
facts tended to indicate the need for some kind of protective supervision
concerning Mr Z., i.e. tutorship, curatorship or advisorhip: see articles 256
C.C.Q. and following.

[
78
]

Mr S. testified that Mr Z.'s house was not in
good shape and that Mr Z.'s financial situation no longer allowed him to stay
there. He added that the trust fund had been depleted to a certain extent due
to Mr Z.'s divorce, as some $30,000 or $40,000 had been used to purchase Mr Z.'s
wife's interest in the residence.

[
79
]

Thus, something had to be done and Mr S. had
hoped that through the Hospital's motion, Mr Z. could be gotten out of his
house.

[
80
]

At the end of the proceedings, when taking the
Hospital's motion under advisement, the Court pointed out that protective
supervision proceedings could be undertaken without waiting for the present
judgment.

Conclusions

[
81
]

The Court:

DISMISSES
the Motion for authorization
of medical treatment;

Without costs.
